tagline: Mineral springs and prehistoric bones on a Boone County parkway
intro: Big Bone Lick/Middle Creek Parkway links Beaverlick with Commissary Corner along four Kentucky routes in Boone County. The state’s scenic-highway inventory records a 19.931-mile corridor designated on May 24, 1995. Belleview lies along the Ohio River, while Big Bone Creek flows through the state park before joining the river. The surrounding East Bend country includes Ohio River bottomland and farmland on the Kentucky side, opposite high rocky hills in Indiana.

At Big Bone, water passing through limestone and shale brings dissolved salts to the surface. The springs supported a salt-making venture in 1809, but the weak brine required 500 to 600 gallons of water for one bushel of salt. The venture failed by 1812. A later preservation effort began when local historical groups pursued a park; the Big Bone Lick Historical Association bought land in 1956 and deeded it to the state for conservation.

From the Woolper Road end at Commissary Corner, follow the corridor toward Belleview on KY 18. The journey continues through Rabbit Hash toward Big Bone Lick. At the park, the Discovery Trail passes through grassland, wetland and savanna, with a boardwalk beside recreated prehistoric animals. The drive finishes at Beaverlick, where KY 338 meets US 42.

moments.title: Rabbit Hash
moments.text: Rabbit Hash’s canine elections have helped rebuild its best-known landmark. The hamlet, formerly Carlton, changed its name because mail was being confused with Carrollton farther down the Ohio. Its first elected dog mayor took office in 1998. The store had been listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1989, before the wider historic district received recognition in 2003. When the historic General Store burned in 2016, only three walls and the floor survived. The election that year raised almost $9,000 for restoration. The store reopened in April 2017, rebuilt on its original foundation with surviving material and donated period lumber.

moments.title: Big Bone Lick State Park
moments.text: Big Bone Lick’s fossils helped naturalists distinguish mastodons from mammoths. Meriwether Lewis collected bones here in late 1803, but they were lost or stolen. In 1807 William Clark removed more than 300 bones and teeth and sent them to Thomas Jefferson with an eleven-page description. Mammoths are believed to have come for salt deposited near the sulfur springs. The park’s Discovery Trail now includes a marsh-bog diorama with recreated mammoth, mastodon and ground sloth figures; a small living bison herd is maintained on-site. Indoor and outdoor visitor-center exhibits include fossils and a 1,000-pound mastodon skull.
moments.notice: The Discovery Trail’s marsh-bog diorama includes recreations of a woolly mammoth, mastodon and ground sloth.

moments.title: Beaverlick
moments.text: Beaverlick grew from a fur-trading site into a community with two blacksmiths, a carriage maker, a flour mill and three churches. The village also supported two physicians and a millinery shop, alongside the hotel and general store that served its earlier community. Its name comes from its location at the source of the Beaver Branch of Big Bone Creek. The post office opened in 1854 and closed in 1944. Historic houses, churches and cemeteries remain from the village. Here Kentucky Route 338 meets US 42 at the parkway’s Beaverlick endpoint.
